title: Segmentation
summary: Dividing memory by logical meaning — code, data, stack — instead of fixed size, and why real systems combine segmentation with paging rather than picking one.

slides.markdown:
Paging chops memory into uniform, meaningless fixed-size pieces. **Segmentation** takes the opposite view: divide memory according to how the *programmer* actually thinks about it — one segment for code, one for the stack, one for the heap — each sized to whatever that logical unit needs.

This buys natural per-segment protection (code segments can be read-only and executable, stack segments read/write) and clean sharing (two processes running the same library share one code segment), but it reintroduces variable-size allocation, and with it, external fragmentation. That trade-off is exactly why almost nobody uses pure segmentation today — and why the topic is really about *segmentation with paging*, the hybrid nearly every real system landed on.

slides.sectionTitle: Segmentation: memory divided by logical meaning, not fixed size
slides.markdown:
In **segmentation**, a program's address space isn't one flat range of bytes — it's a collection of separately-sized, separately-protected segments, and every address is really a pair: `(segment number, offset within that segment)`.

This maps naturally onto how compilers already think about a program: code lives in one region, global/static data in another, the stack grows in a third, the heap in a fourth. Each of those becomes its own segment, sized to exactly what it needs — a 2 KB code segment and a 10 MB heap segment can coexist without either one wasting space to match the other's size, unlike a fixed-size paging scheme.

slides.sectionTitle: Segments: code, data, stack, heap as separate units
slides.markdown:
A typical process has at least four segments, each with its own purpose and its own protection bits:

- **Code (text) segment** — the compiled instructions. Usually read-only and executable, so a bug can't accidentally overwrite the program's own logic.
- **Data segment** — global and static variables. Read/write, not executable.
- **Heap segment** — dynamically allocated memory (`malloc`), grows upward as the program requests more.
- **Stack segment** — function call frames and local variables, grows downward, one per thread.

Giving each of these its own segment means the hardware can enforce "code can't be written to" and "the stack can't be executed" as a property of *which segment* an address falls in, not something the program has to check itself.

slides.sectionTitle: The segment table: base and limit per segment
slides.markdown:
Where a flat base/limit scheme has exactly one base and one limit for the whole process, segmentation gives each process a **segment table** — one base/limit pair *per segment*, indexed by segment number.

Translating an address is: look up entry `segment_number` in the table to get that segment's base and limit, check the offset against the limit (trap if it's out of bounds), then compute `physical = base + offset`. It's the same arithmetic as the single-segment case, just repeated per-segment with an extra lookup step first — which is also where segmentation's per-segment protection bits (read/write/execute) naturally live, one set per table entry.

slides.sectionTitle: Protection and sharing benefits of segmentation
slides.markdown:
Because each segment table entry carries its own permission bits, segmentation gives protection *for free* at the hardware level: mark the code segment read+execute, the data and stack segments read+write, and any attempt to jump into the stack or write to code traps immediately — no software check required.

Sharing gets similarly clean: if two processes run the same shared library, they can each have a segment table entry that points at the *same* physical base — one copy of the code in RAM, referenced by two (or a thousand) processes, each with their own private data and stack segments. Paging can share pages too, but segmentation's whole-logical-unit granularity makes "share this entire library" a much more natural one-entry operation.

slides.sectionTitle: External fragmentation returns with pure segmentation
slides.markdown:
Segments are variable-size by design — that's the whole point, sizing each one to what it logically needs — which means pure segmentation is placing variable-size blocks in physical memory, exactly the problem contiguous allocation had. A heap segment that needs to grow might not have free space immediately after it; a new process's stack segment has to fit somewhere among existing holes.

So segmentation solves the *logical* organization problem (natural protection and sharing boundaries) while reintroducing the *physical* placement problem external fragmentation causes. This is the core reason pure segmentation never became the dominant approach in general-purpose OSes — it traded one hard problem for another instead of eliminating it.

The practical answer nearly every real architecture converged on: **segment the address space for logical organization and protection, then page each segment internally** to avoid needing it to be physically contiguous.

An address becomes three parts: `(segment number, page number within that segment, offset within that page)`. The segment table entry now points to a *page table* for that segment, rather than a raw physical base — so the code segment can be scattered across non-contiguous frames just like anything else, while still being one coherent logical unit with one set of protection bits. x86's classic segmented+paged model (still present, though mostly vestigial in 64-bit mode) worked exactly this way; most modern OSes on x86-64 use paging almost exclusively and treat segments as flat, near-unused artifacts of the architecture.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: segmentation vs paging — logical vs physical view of memory
slides.markdown:
| | Segmentation | Paging |
|---|---|---|
| Unit size | Variable, matches logical structure | Fixed, arbitrary boundary |
| What the unit represents | Something meaningful to the program (code, stack, heap) | Nothing — just a fixed chunk of address space |
| Internal fragmentation | No | Yes, bounded by page size |
| External fragmentation | Yes | No |
| Natural fit for | Per-region protection, whole-library sharing | Physical placement flexibility, demand loading |
| Programmer/compiler visibility | Segments often align with source-level structure | Pages are invisible to the programmer |

The honest framing: segmentation answers "how should memory be organized to match how programs are structured," paging answers "how should memory be placed physically without fragmenting." They're solving different problems, which is exactly why combining them (previous slide) made sense instead of picking a winner.

slides.sectionTitle: Where segmentation's ideas live on today
slides.markdown:
Even though pure segmentation is largely gone from mainstream 64-bit OSes, its core idea — give logically distinct regions their own protection, independent of physical placement — is everywhere. A modern process's page table entries carry per-page read/write/execute bits, which is segmentation's protection idea implemented at page granularity instead of segment granularity: **NX (no-execute) bits** mark stack and heap pages non-executable specifically to block stack-overflow-based code injection, and read-only mappings protect the code and constant-data regions.

Shared libraries (`.so`/`.dll` files) are the direct descendant of segment-based sharing: one physical copy of `libc`'s code pages, mapped read-only into every process that links it, each process still getting its own private data. The segment table is mostly gone; the ideas it introduced became per-page attributes instead.
